title: How do you debug a Spark OOM (OutOfMemoryError) — check Spark UI (Stages tab for task duration spread, Executors tab for GC time, Storage tab for cache size, SQL tab for plan), look for data skew (one task much larger), excessive shuffle, large broadcast, too few partitions, or driver OOM from `collect()`?
shortTitle: How to debug a Spark OutOfMemoryError

s1_definition.profdef: Debugging a Spark OutOfMemoryError is a systematic process of locating which component ran out of memory — an executor or the driver — and which cause produced it, using the Spark UI as the primary evidence source. You check the Stages tab for a wide spread in task duration or shuffle size that signals skew, the Executors tab for high garbage-collection time and failed tasks that signal memory pressure, the Storage tab for oversized cached data, and the SQL tab for a plan with a large broadcast or an unexpectedly expensive wide operation. The common root causes are data skew concentrating a huge partition on one task, excessive shuffle, a broadcast of a table that is too large, too few partitions making each one too big, and driver-side OOM from pulling data back with operations like collect.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India an OutOfMemory error is like a clerk's desk overflowing with paperwork until they collapse. Debugging it is detective work: you first ask whether it was a field clerk (executor) or the head manager (driver) who collapsed, then you check the activity logs (Spark UI) — was one clerk handed a mountain of slips while others sat idle (skew), was everyone drowning in paperwork being shuffled between desks (excessive shuffle), was a huge reference binder copied to every desk (large broadcast), were there too few desks so each pile was enormous (too few partitions), or did the manager try to pile the entire bank's records onto their own desk at once (driver collect)?
s1_definition.oneliner: Debug a Spark OOM by finding whether the driver or an executor died and why — use the UI's Stages, Executors, Storage, and SQL tabs to spot skew, excessive shuffle, oversized broadcast, too few partitions, or a driver-side collect.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Debugging a Spark OutOfMemoryError is a systematic process of locating which component ran out of memory — an executor or the driver — and which cause produced it, using the Spark UI as the primary evidence source. You check the Stages tab for a wide spread in task duration or shuffle size that signals skew, the Executors tab for high garbage-collection time and failed tasks that signal memory pressure, the Storage tab for oversized cached data, and the SQL tab for a plan with a large broadcast or an unexpectedly expensive wide operation. The common root causes are data skew concentrating a huge partition on one task, excessive shuffle, a broadcast of a table that is too large, too few partitions making each one too big, and driver-side OOM from pulling data back with operations like collect.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India an OutOfMemory error is like a clerk's desk overflowing with paperwork until they collapse. Debugging it is detective work: you first ask whether it was a field clerk (executor) or the head manager (driver) who collapsed, then you check the activity logs (Spark UI) — was one clerk handed a mountain of slips while others sat idle (skew), was everyone drowning in paperwork being shuffled between desks (excessive shuffle), was a huge reference binder copied to every desk (large broadcast), were there too few desks so each pile was enormous (too few partitions), or did the manager try to pile the entire bank's records onto their own desk at once (driver collect)?

**One line to remember:** Debug a Spark OOM by finding whether the driver or an executor died and why — use the UI's Stages, Executors, Storage, and SQL tabs to spot skew, excessive shuffle, oversized broadcast, too few partitions, or a driver-side collect.

sections.s2_technical:
The first question is driver versus executor. A driver OOM almost always comes from pulling large data back to the driver — calling collect on a big DataFrame, a toPandas, a huge broadcast being assembled, or accumulating results in a driver-side structure. The fix is to never collect large results; write to storage instead, and if you must bring data back, take or limit it. An executor OOM comes from a task's working set exceeding available execution memory, and that is where the richer investigation applies.

Data skew is the most common executor OOM cause. In the Stages tab you look at the task metrics: if the maximum task duration and the maximum shuffle read are many times the median, one partition is far larger than the rest and that task is running out of memory. The fix is the skew toolkit — enable AQE skew join, salt the hot key, or isolate and broadcast it. Skew is identifiable precisely because the UI shows a lopsided distribution across tasks in the same stage.

Excessive shuffle and too few partitions are related. A wide operation that moves enormous data, visible as large shuffle read and write in the Stages tab, strains execution memory, and if the number of shuffle partitions is too low, each partition is too big to fit, causing spills and then OOM. The fix is to increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions so each partition is smaller, and to reduce shuffle volume by pre-aggregating or pruning columns before the shuffle. Conversely far too many tiny partitions waste overhead, so you aim for a sensible partition size, often in the low hundreds of megabytes.

A large broadcast is a subtle cause. If a join broadcasts a table that turns out larger than expected — because statistics were stale or autoBroadcastJoinThreshold was raised — every executor must hold the whole table, and the driver must assemble it first, so you can OOM on either side. The SQL tab shows a BroadcastExchange and the broadcast size; if that table is big, you disable the broadcast for that join or lower the threshold. High garbage-collection time in the Executors tab is a general pressure signal: when GC time is a large fraction of task time, the executor is thrashing near its memory limit and is close to OOM, often because of one of the above causes plus over-caching.

A senior-level nuance is the disciplined order of investigation and the distinction between a configuration fix and a logic fix. You first identify driver or executor from the error and logs, then open the Stages tab to check the task distribution, the Executors tab for GC and failures, the Storage tab for cache size, and the SQL tab for the plan. Only after the evidence points to a cause do you act: raising executor memory or partition count is a configuration fix that helps genuine volume problems but merely masks skew, whereas skew, an accidental collect, or an oversized broadcast are logic problems that need a code change. The mistake juniors make is to throw more memory at every OOM; the senior approach is to read the UI, classify the cause, and apply the matching fix.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a transactions job that OOMs. The Stages tab shows one task with shuffle read fifty times the median: classic skew on a pooling account, needing the skew toolkit, not more memory.

Problem 2 — A report OOMs on the driver. The code calls collect on a multi-million-row DataFrame. The fix is to write to storage instead of collecting.

Problem 3 — A join OOMs because a reference table assumed small is actually large and is being broadcast to every executor. The fix is to stop broadcasting that table.

The demo models a small diagnostic engine that takes OOM symptoms — where it died and key UI metrics — and classifies the likely cause and recommended fix, logging the reasoning so an on-call engineer has a checklist.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four OOM cases with their location and key metrics — an executor OOM with a skew ratio of fifty, a driver OOM with collect called, an executor OOM with a four-hundred-megabyte broadcast, and an executor OOM with no skew or broadcast.

Step 1: The txn-join executor case enters. It is not the driver, and its max-to-median task ratio of fifty is well above the skew threshold, so the diagnoser classifies it as data skew and recommends the skew toolkit.

Step 2: The daily-report driver case enters. It is a driver OOM and collect was called, so the diagnoser classifies it as a collect problem and recommends writing to storage instead.

Step 3: The ref-join executor case enters. No skew, but the broadcast size of four hundred megabytes exceeds the large-broadcast threshold, so the diagnoser classifies it as an oversized broadcast and recommends disabling the broadcast for that join.

Step 4: The wide-agg executor case enters. No skew, small broadcast, so the diagnoser falls through to too-few-partitions or heavy shuffle and recommends raising shuffle partitions and pruning before the shuffle.

Final output:


sections.s6_takeaway:
Debugging a Spark OutOfMemoryError is systematic detective work, and my first step is always to determine whether the driver or an executor ran out of memory, because the causes are different. A driver OOM is almost always from pulling large data back to the driver — a collect, a toPandas, assembling a huge broadcast, or accumulating in a driver-side structure — and the fix is to write results to storage instead of collecting them. An executor OOM is a task's working set exceeding execution memory, and that is where I use the Spark UI in earnest.

In the UI I check four tabs. The Stages tab shows the task duration and shuffle-size distribution, and a maximum many times the median means data skew concentrating a giant partition on one task, which I fix with AQE skew join, salting, or isolate-and-broadcast rather than more memory. The Executors tab shows garbage-collection time and failed tasks, and a high GC fraction means the executor is thrashing near its limit. The Storage tab shows cached data size, because over-caching steals memory that joins need and shows up as spilling. The SQL tab shows the plan, where an unexpectedly large BroadcastExchange reveals a table being broadcast that is too big, which I fix by disabling that broadcast or lowering the threshold. When none of those apply, the cause is usually too few shuffle partitions making each one too large, fixed by raising the partition count and pruning before the shuffle.

At the National Bank of India this playbook resolved real incidents: a transactions join that OOMed turned out to be skew on a pooling account, visible as one task with fifty times the median shuffle read; a daily report that crashed the driver was a collect on millions of rows; and a join that OOMed every executor was broadcasting a reference table that had grown large. The lesson I stress in interviews is that the junior reflex of adding memory to every OOM only masks skew and accidental collects, whereas the senior approach is to read the UI, classify the cause as either a configuration problem or a logic problem, and apply the matching fix.
